title: Getting started with ChatGPT
description: Start a conversation, choose a useful first task, and learn when to move from a quick chat to a larger task in Work. Includes voice basics and a route into the AI Foundations course.
bestFor: Your first conversations with ChatGPT
needs: No programming required.

title: Elements of AI
description: An introduction to what AI is, what it can do, and how to think about its effects. A useful foundation before focusing on a particular tool.
bestFor: Understanding AI beyond a single product
needs: An account is required for complete course access. Six chapters with exercises; check the course FAQ for completion requirements.

title: Wharton Prompt Library
description: Reusable prompts with guidance for testing and adapting them. Includes an idea-challenging “Devil’s Advocate” example and a practical checklist for evaluating outputs.
bestFor: Improving a prompt you actually use
needs: Test prompts with your own tasks and model. Reusing the library’s prompts requires attribution to Ethan and Lilach Mollick under CC BY 4.0.

title: Google AI Essentials
description: Hands-on practice in prompting, workplace tasks, and responsible use. A structured option for people who want a short course with a completion certificate.
credential: Google completion certificate; not a professional license.
needs: No technical experience required. Google lists US/Canada pricing at US$49 per month after a 7-day trial; check local enrollment pricing.
bestFor: A structured introduction to AI at work

title: AI concepts for developers and technology professionals
description: A beginner learning path with seven modules covering core AI concepts, generative AI and agents, language, speech, vision, information extraction, and retrieval-augmented generation. Assumes basic computing and math knowledge.
bestFor: Technical beginners who want a guided AI overview
needs: Basic computing and math knowledge; aimed at developers and AI engineers.

title: Generative AI for Beginners
description: A 21-lesson curriculum with Python and TypeScript examples: chat, search, images, retrieval, agents, and application security.
needs: Python or TypeScript fundamentals. Foundry Local offers an offline route without a cloud subscription. Cloud examples may incur usage charges; the course directs former GitHub Models exercises to Microsoft Foundry Models. Follow its setup guide.
bestFor: Building a foundation through working examples

title: OpenAI Cookbook
description: Practical examples and guides for building with the OpenAI API. Start with a use case and work through the accompanying code.
bestFor: Finding an implementation pattern
needs: Coding experience; examples are mostly Python. API examples require an OpenAI account, API key and any billed model usage.

title: AI Agents Course
description: Learn agent concepts, work with established frameworks, and build an evaluated final project. Includes retrieval, observability, and a game-playing example.
needs: Basic Python and LLM knowledge; a Hugging Face account for publishing projects.
credential: Free course certificates: a fundamentals certificate after Unit 1, and a completion certificate after the required use case and final challenge.
bestFor: Building agents and learning to observe and evaluate them

title: Hugging Face Learn
description: Courses on language models, agents, robotics and audio, plus an open-source cookbook. Choose a subject and check the course prerequisites before starting.
bestFor: Exploring additional technical subjects

title: Make repeated API context cost less
description: Learn how repeated API calls reuse the beginning of a prompt. Use the guide’s usage fields to check for cache hits and compare the cost of an initial write with later reads.
needs: An API integration with repeated context. Rates and cache behavior vary by model; a persistent session does not guarantee a cache hit.
bestFor: Reducing avoidable latency and input costs

title: Gemini Notebook / NotebookLM
description: Work with a collection of documents and ask questions tied to those sources. Useful for comparing readings and tracing a summary back to the underlying material.
needs: Google account. Free tier: up to 50 sources per notebook. Drive sources sync; other imports can become stale. Updating a source does not refresh already-generated Studio outputs. Web imports omit images and nested pages; YouTube uses captions, not visuals, and videos under 72 hours old may fail. Verify citations against originals.
bestFor: Reading a stack of sources

title: Zotero
description: Collect, annotate, organize, and cite original research. A useful companion to AI reading tools when you need a durable source library.
cost: Free app · optional paid file storage
needs: Desktop app or browser connector. Optional file syncing includes 300 MB free; larger storage plans cost extra. This is a reference manager, not a generative AI model.
bestFor: Keeping the evidence behind your work

title: n8n
description: Run a workflow when an app sends an event, then pass the result to another app or model. Cloud pricing counts runs of the whole workflow, so a ten-step run counts as one execution.
cost: Paid cloud by workflow execution · self-host options
needs: App credentials and workflow setup. Cloud bills by workflow run; Assistant credits and model usage have separate allowances. Trials are limited. History limits remove old logs rather than stop workflows; paid self-hosted quotas can incur overages. Check license terms before reselling.
bestFor: Connecting AI to the apps you use

title: LM Studio / Bionic
description: Explore open models on your own computer through a desktop interface. Its Bionic agent also supports document and coding work.
needs: Hardware requirements depend on the model. Local inference is free; optional Bionic+ starts at US$20/month. Cloud models and web tools send data off your device, so check which mode you are using.
bestFor: Experimenting with local models

title: ChatGPT Ads for Shopify
description: Sync a Shopify catalog with ChatGPT Ads Manager, build campaigns from product listings and measure conversions with the Shopify pixel. Check its data permissions before connecting a store.
bestFor: Merchants evaluating a new advertising channel
needs: A Shopify store and an eligible ChatGPT Ads account. OpenAI announced 89-country availability on October 21; check your market. The listing requests customer data and pixel access. Test syncing, set a small spend limit and check conversion results before expanding; installation is free, campaigns are not.

title: AI Town
description: A virtual village where AI characters talk and socialize. An open-source starting point for experimenting with simulated worlds; supports several model providers, including OpenAI-compatible APIs.
imageAlt: Editorial pixel illustration of a small village among green trees
bestFor: Exploring playful agent simulations
needs: JavaScript/TypeScript, Convex (cloud or self-hosted), and a model provider; local Ollama is supported. README setup instructions include older runtimes: review dependencies before running. Model changes can require resetting stored embeddings; back up data first. Source reviewed, not run by us.

title: A document summarization workflow
description: An inspectable template collection for summarizing URLs, text, and PDFs. Adapt one input path first, then compare its summaries with the original documents.
needs: n8n and model API credentials; optional OCR.Space for scanned PDFs. The template names GPT-4.1-mini, so check model availability before importing. Restrict webhook access and test each input path with non-sensitive files. Template reviewed, not run by us.
bestFor: Turning a repetitive reading task into a workflow

title: Build a demo with Gradio
description: Turn a Python function or model into a small web interface. The README includes a minimal working example and options for sharing a demo.
needs: Python 3.10 or later. Model and hosting costs vary. Enabling share=True creates a public URL even when computation runs on your computer; review access before sharing.
bestFor: Making an experiment usable by someone else

title: Build a browser voice agent
description: A current TypeScript starting point for a browser voice assistant, using the Agents SDK and WebRTC. Covers connection setup, microphone audio and a first conversation.
needs: Node.js/TypeScript, Zod v4 and OpenAI API access. Keep the regular API key on a backend; use short-lived client tokens in the browser. Source reviewed, not run by this site.
bestFor: Starting a new voice project with current APIs

title: Realtime Console
description: An example for exploring the Realtime API with WebRTC, event logging and client-side function calls. A useful reference for understanding voice interactions.
bestFor: Understanding realtime events and voice interactions
needs: Node.js and an OpenAI API key. Last repository push: August 2025; check current model availability and dependencies before running it. Not tested by this site.

title: Realtime voice agents
description: A Next.js reference for chat-supervisor and sequential-handoff voice patterns. Its sample session still requests a retired Realtime preview model, so it needs migration before use.
needs: Node.js, TypeScript and paid API access. The sample requests gpt-4o-realtime-preview-2025-06-03, listed as shut down May 7, 2026. Use the current voice quickstart for a new project. Source reviewed; demo not run.
bestFor: Studying voice-agent supervision and handoff patterns

title: Hugging Face Spaces
description: A directory of community AI demos across text, images, audio, and code. Individual projects vary in quality, maintenance, and data handling; inclusion is a discovery link, not an endorsement.
bestFor: Discovering and trying community experiments
needs: Check each demo’s author, code and data practices before uploading files. For hosting, static Spaces are free; creating Gradio or Docker Spaces generally requires a paid plan, with a limited ZeroGPU exception for eligible personal accounts. Protected source code does not make the running app private.

title: Make Real
description: A sketch-to-interface project built with the tldraw SDK. The repository was archived on February 20, 2026; treat it as a reference rather than an actively maintained starter. Its README links to a separate starter repository.
imageAlt: Editorial pixel illustration of sketches turning into an interface
bestFor: Studying a sketch-to-interface experiment
needs: Archived reference; use the README’s separate starter link for follow-up research.

title: Test the business before you build
description: Market research, business-plan examples, startup costs, and break-even planning in one reference. Use it to define a customer and a deliverable before investing in an AI service.
bestFor: Validating a service or product idea

title: Choosing a pricing model
description: Compare subscriptions, usage-based billing, tiers, and hybrid models. Useful for a software product whose model and support costs change with customer usage.
bestFor: Pricing an AI software product
needs: Commercial guidance from a payments provider; adapt the examples to your own costs and customer research.

title: Fyxer: an assistant business
description: A vendor case study on splitting email assistance into smaller jobs, testing drafts against real tasks, and using edits as feedback. Useful product-design lessons; retention and revenue figures are company-reported.
bestFor: Studying a focused subscription product

title: Harvey: software for a specific profession
description: A September 2026 case study of legal drafting with source context and lawyers’ preferences. Read it for how a specialist product organizes documents and review; the claimed improvements are reported by the vendor.
bestFor: Understanding a vertical software business
needs: Vendor account, not independently audited business results. Professional applications require appropriate expertise and review.

title: Stanford AI Index
description: The 2026 report brings together evidence on AI adoption, investment, capabilities and governance. Use the data and methods to test a market story; aggregate trends do not prove demand for your particular service.
bestFor: Checking a market story against broader evidence

title: International AI Safety Report 2026
description: A scientific synthesis of general-purpose AI capabilities, emerging risks, and risk management. Its authors distinguish evidence from uncertainty; the report does not endorse a particular policy.

safety.why: A broad scientific synthesis is a useful foundation before reading individual claims about AI risk.
safety.readFirst: Start with the executive summary, then follow the chapter behind a claim.
safety.limits: Published February 2026; its evidence predates later model releases and incidents. A synthesis is not a prediction that every scenario will occur. We reviewed the executive summary, not every underlying study.

title: AI Incident Database
description: A searchable index of reported real-world AI harms and near harms. Follow the underlying sources for context and the status of individual claims; an indexed report is not a final finding.

safety.why: Connects abstract debates to reported harms and the sources behind them.
safety.readFirst: Search for a use case you recognize and open the underlying reports.
safety.limits: An indexed incident is not a final finding, and report counts do not measure the prevalence of harm.

title: AI Risk Management Framework
description: Voluntary guidance for managing AI risks across the life of a system, with links to a companion Playbook and generative AI profile. NIST notes that version 1.0 is being revised.

safety.why: A practical framework for assigning responsibility and reviewing risks across an AI system’s life.
safety.readFirst: Use the companion Playbook to turn a risk discussion into specific actions.
safety.limits: Voluntary guidance, not certification or proof that a system is safe. Version 1.0 is being revised.

title: AI Now Institute
description: Research and policy advocacy examining AI companies, concentrated power, and public accountability.

safety.why: Examines who holds power, who bears costs, and how public institutions could respond.
safety.readFirst: Choose a topic in its research library, then examine the evidence behind its policy recommendations.
safety.limits: Research and advocacy from an organization with a stated policy agenda; examine the evidence behind each proposal.

title: PauseAI
description: The case for pausing development of the most powerful AI systems, alongside policy proposals and ways to get involved. This is an advocacy organization.

safety.why: A direct source for the argument to pause the development of the most powerful AI systems.
safety.readFirst: Read the proposal and its scope before deciding whether to support a campaign.
safety.limits: An advocacy position. Its claims and proposed remedies should be assessed separately.

title: METR evaluations
description: Independent evaluations of AI capabilities and safeguards. Its November 5 review examines how Anthropic judged the risk of AI accelerating its own research.

safety.why: Empirical evaluations help distinguish measured capabilities from claims about what agents can do.
safety.readFirst: Read the executive summary, then compare METR’s assessment of the early warning threshold with Anthropic’s explanation.
safety.limits: The November review examines conclusions about July models in an August risk report. Anthropic could redact nonpublic information. Check the redaction summary before interpreting the findings.

title: Apollo Research
description: Technical work on model deception, scheming, and alignment evaluations. Study findings describe tested conditions; they do not establish the prevalence of a behavior in everyday use.

safety.why: Studies model deception and behavior that standard usefulness benchmarks can miss.
safety.readFirst: Compare the scheming studies with the system-card evaluation summaries. Check whether models recognized the tests and what the baselines were.
safety.limits: Behavior elicited in an evaluation does not establish how frequently it happens in deployment.

title: AI Security Institute
provider: UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
description: Government research on advanced AI capabilities, public safety, and risk mitigations, alongside evaluation tools and technical reports.

safety.why: Offers government-led evaluations and research on advanced AI capabilities and safeguards.
safety.readFirst: Compare a capability study’s tasks, model access and limits. The open-weight cyber analysis distinguishes short tasks from longer simulated networks; those ranges lack some real-world defenses.
safety.limits: A UK government perspective. Evaluation results depend on access, methods, and the systems tested.

title: MIT AI Risk Repository
description: A structured collection of AI risks and the frameworks that describe them. Useful for checking whether a discussion overlooks social, security, or system-level harms.

safety.why: A map of risk categories helps reveal what a narrow discussion leaves out.
safety.readFirst: Start with the risk repository, then use the Risk Navigator to connect risk categories with incidents and governance records.
safety.limits: A catalog organizes risks; it does not establish that every risk is equally likely or severe.

title: Epoch AI
description: Data explorers and research on model capabilities, compute, and AI infrastructure. Check measurement methods, coverage, and assumptions before comparing claims.

safety.why: Makes claims about capabilities and compute easier to inspect against underlying measurements.
safety.readFirst: Compare the model-capability and data-center explorers, then read the definitions, coverage and uncertainty behind the numbers.
safety.limits: Benchmarks and compute estimates have assumptions; projections are not observations.

title: Privacy considerations with AI tools
description: A readable guide to what happens to your data in AI apps, integrations, and local or cloud tools. Covers privacy settings, retention, and the limits of “private” modes.

safety.why: Helps you make a concrete decision about what information to share with an AI tool.
safety.readFirst: Start by auditing extensions and connected apps, then check privacy settings and retention. Revoke access you no longer want.
safety.limits: Advice from a digital-rights organization. Product settings change; follow its links to current provider documentation.

title: AI and cyber security: what you need to know
description: A nontechnical introduction to AI security for managers: unreliable outputs, attacks on AI systems, sensitive data, and responsibility within an organization.

safety.why: Gives people responsible for adopting AI a way to discuss security with their teams.
safety.readFirst: Use the questions for managers to identify who owns AI security and how your organization would respond to a serious incident.
safety.limits: A security overview, not a complete treatment of social risks; some product examples reflect an earlier generation of tools.

title: Measure whether AI is paying off
description: A practical approach to comparing AI use with delivery time, quality and business outcomes. Includes review and correction time, setup and support costs; its ROI example is illustrative, not a measured earnings result.
needs: Useful for team leads and service providers. The product walkthrough uses ChatGPT administrator analytics; verify access in your plan.
bestFor: Evaluating a workflow before expanding it

title: Dots: access and approvals
description: Understand cloud computers, app connections and the boundary between background research and actions. Review Custom Rules before assigning consequential work.
cost: Free guide · Eligible paid plan required
bestFor: Deciding what an always-on agent may do
needs: Check your plan, region and workspace settings. Eligible Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare admins can opt in or out during the preview before November 18. Review who can use dots and which apps they can access.

title: Choose a model and measure the result
description: A practical guide to balancing model capability, latency and cost, with advice on instructions, long-running work and production checks. Test vendor recommendations on your own tasks.
needs: Basic API or coding-agent experience. The October 2 overview predates GPT-6.1 Terra; use the current developer guide for model-specific details. Compare cost per successful task and test before changing a production workflow.
bestFor: Choosing a model for a real workload

title: Put a spending limit on an AWS project
description: A guide to setting a monthly project spending ceiling that pauses resources when reached. Useful for experiments that create cloud infrastructure; compare a real stop with a notification-only budget alert.
bestFor: Containing cloud costs during agent experiments
needs: For the new AWS account experience; requires a Paid Plan and project-owner access. Minimum cap is $20 or a higher usage estimate, before tax. Pausing interrupts services; after 90 days without action, paused project data is permanently deleted. Optional early controls can also block new resources or pause idle or high-cost resources before the ceiling.

title: ChatGPT for Teens risk assessment
provider: Common Sense Media · Youth AI Safety Institute
description: An October 7 assessment of teen safeguards, with its testing methods and findings. Read the original evidence and stated limits; OpenAI disputes the evaluation.

safety.why: Adds a focused evaluation of a product many young people use, rather than relying on launch assurances.
safety.readFirst: Read the methodology and limitations before the findings. Compare the report with OpenAI’s documentation and response.
safety.limits: Testing ended September 28, before the October GPT-6 launch and October 30 safeguard announcement; it does not evaluate those changes. US-based sequential tests, with model changes complicating comparisons and some modes excluded. The institute reports industry funding including the OpenAI Foundation and editorial independence. We have not reproduced the tests.

title: Release AI mathematics responsibly
provider: Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence
description: Calls for labs to stop testing advanced mathematics on inaccessible proprietary models, alongside recommendations for attribution, proof artifacts and community-led human understanding when results are released.
bestFor: Evaluating how AI research claims are shared
needs: Mathematical research context. These are scholarly recommendations, not verification of any particular proof or endorsement of a lab.

title: AI agents: access and evaluation controls
description: Practical guidance for keeping agent evaluations away from live systems, protecting credentials and detecting unauthorized activity.
bestFor: Setting enforceable limits on agents

safety.why: Connects reported failures to specific controls.
safety.readFirst: Start with the actions for your role: enforce network limits outside the model, use synthetic targets, and define an automatic stop.
safety.limits: The advisory does not name affected providers or organizations. Guidance is not proof of universal protection.

title: AI adoption in financial services
description: Twelve practices for financial institutions adopting AI, from accountable leadership and documented uses to oversight and outside-provider risk.
bestFor: Teams building AI for financial services
needs: Read the introduction and twelve-practice summary first. Non-binding guidance, not certification; local obligations still apply. Agent-specific practices remain nascent. We reviewed the introduction and summary, not all case studies.

title: AI for developing economies
description: An overview of AI adoption, local needs, infrastructure and supplier dependence in developing economies. A broader lens for judging where an AI service could be useful.
bestFor: Assessing local needs and adoption constraints
needs: Start with chapter 3 on adapting tools to local conditions. Ask what local data, language coverage and infrastructure a service needs. The overview gives the Bank’s recommendations, not a guarantee of returns.

title: Check your ChatGPT API credit benefit
description: Eligible Pro and Business subscriptions can claim API credits for a linked API organization. Read the activation and expiry rules before budgeting an experiment; these credits do not raise ChatGPT or signed-in Codex usage limits.
cost: Paid eligible subscription · included API credit benefit
bestFor: Using an existing subscription benefit for API experiments
needs: An eligible paid subscription must be active for seven days; account email, API organization ownership and billing access matter. Business credits are pooled: up to $500 per monthly cycle or $6,000 per prepaid year. First grants are prorated; unused credits expire. A workspace seat alone gives no API project access. Paid credits or Auto Recharge can cover later usage.

title: Understand ChatGPT parental controls
description: How linked accounts, quiet hours, study settings and limited notifications work. A practical starting point for a family conversation about using ChatGPT.

safety.why: Explains which settings families can change and what a parent cannot see or monitor.
safety.readFirst: Compare quiet hours, which block access, with study hours, which start eligible chats in study mode. Review the separate controls for code network access and the cloud browser.
safety.limits: Company documentation, not an independent safety assessment. Linking requires acceptance, either side can unlink, and parents cannot read chats. Alerts are limited, may be delayed and will not identify every concern.

title: Verify a suspicious voice or video call
description: Steps for checking an urgent request from someone who sounds familiar, and what to do if money has already moved.

safety.audience: Households and people who approve payments
safety.why: Offers a way to check a caller’s identity even when a recording sounds convincing.
safety.readFirst: Go to the protection tips. Hang up and use contact details you obtained independently. For a transfer already sent, follow the bank-recall and reporting steps in the companion guide.
safety.limits: The reporting route is for the United States. A bank may be able to recall a transfer, but recovery is uncertain.

title: Decide when to use ChatGPT Lockdown Mode
description: A guide to limiting where ChatGPT can send data when you work with sensitive material. Check which features you give up and which privacy settings you still need.

safety.audience: People handling confidential files and workspace administrators
safety.why: Helps you decide whether a particular task needs live web or app access.
safety.readFirst: Read the list of restricted features. For managed workspaces, check the separate rules for apps and their write permissions.
safety.limits: Availability depends on your account. The setting leaves training preferences and Codex network access unchanged. An uploaded file can still contain instructions that influence the answer.

title: Read a U.S. government AI model evaluation
provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology
description: A worked example of how to read a federal model test. See the instructions, tools, scoring rules and uncertainty behind four cybersecurity benchmarks.

safety.why: Shows exactly how much help the researchers gave the model and which comparisons they made.
safety.readFirst: Start with SEC-Bench Pro in the methods table. Compare the clues given to the model with the task you thought the headline described.
safety.limits: Tests one model version in a controlled setting. These results do not establish how often users will face harm in ordinary use.

title: What Australia wants AI labs to report
provider: Australian Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
description: Read the recommendations prompted by the Medicare portal incident. Compare what the reviewers proposed with the safety standards the government says it will legislate.

safety.audience: Readers following AI oversight and incident reporting
safety.why: Shows how a real incident can lead to proposals about reporting deadlines, near misses and regulator powers.
safety.readFirst: Read recommendations 3 and 4 together: one concerns a reporting clock, the other what might encourage people to report near misses.
safety.limits: These are recommendations. Acceptance by the government does not itself create a legal duty or enact a penalty.

title: Read a freelance budget before you bid
description: Compare advertised project budgets, hourly rates and hours actually logged. Exhibit 2.4 separates what clients offer for the whole job from what they offer for an hour.
bestFor: Scoping a freelance project
needs: Results describe one marketplace. Posted budgets are not earnings; estimate your own revisions, testing and delivery time.

title: What New York asks frontier developers to report
description: Read section 1422 of the RAISE Act. It distinguishes critical incidents from routine problems and explains what starts the reporting clock.

safety.audience: Readers comparing AI incident reporting rules
safety.why: Lets you check the actual reporting duties against public claims about them.
safety.readFirst: Compare subdivision 3(a), the ordinary reporting clock, with 3(b), the rule for imminent physical danger.
safety.limits: This section concerns frontier models and defined critical safety incidents. It is not a general consumer complaint process.

title: Make your first image edit in ChatGPT
description: Watch three ways to start: describe a new picture, refine it in conversation, or edit a photo. Try changing one detail at a time so you can see what else changes.
cost: Free to watch · product limits vary
bestFor: Making one deliberate visual change

title: What the Paris AI safety declaration commits to
provider: Government of the Netherlands · declaration text
description: Compare the commitments on independent testing, shutdown mechanisms and incident reporting with what signatory CeSIA still wants made mandatory.

safety.audience: Readers comparing frontier AI safety commitments
safety.why: Puts the declaration next to a signatory’s argument about who should be able to stop a model.
safety.readFirst: Read the second section on evaluation, then compare the language about external access with CeSIA’s response.
safety.limits: A joint declaration does not demonstrate that any particular model has passed an independent test or that regulators can order a shutdown.
